## Before We Start

This is a companion workshop to the slides, with two real data sets. In
each section:

1.  Read the **PREDICT** box and decide what you think will happen.
2.  Run the chunks (click ▶ on each one, in order).
3.  Do the **YOUR TURN** box: change one value, re-run, and compare.

Ridge and the lasso both minimize the residual sum of squares plus a
penalty on the coefficients:

$$\text{Ridge: } \text{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j} \beta_j^2
\qquad\qquad
\text{Lasso: } \text{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j} |\beta_j|$$

In R, `glmnet` fits both. `alpha = 0` gives ridge and `alpha = 1` gives
the lasso. It **standardizes the predictors** before fitting.

```{r}
for (pkg in c("glmnet", "BGLR", "AppliedPredictiveModeling", "ggplot2")) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
}
library(glmnet)   # ridge (alpha = 0) and lasso (alpha = 1)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
```

## 1. Wheat Yield from Genetic Markers

These data come from the wheat breeding program at the International
Maize and Wheat Improvement Center, which tests wheat lines in trials
around the world.

- **Rows:** 599 wheat lines (varieties).
- **Features:** 1,279 genetic markers, scored 0 or 1 to record whether a
  particular stretch of DNA is absent or present.
- **Response:** grain yield shown as an index: 100 is the average line,
  and 10 points is one standard deviation.

We train on 80% of the lines (479) and test on the other 20% (120).

> **PREDICT:** Yield is thought to be shaped by many genes, each with a
> small effect. Which method will predict yield best on the test lines:
> least squares, ridge, or the lasso? Why?

```{r}
library(glmnet)
data(wheat, package = "BGLR")   # loads wheat.X (markers) and wheat.Y (yield)
X <- wheat.X
y <- 100 + 10 * wheat.Y[, 1]    # yield index: 100 = average line, 10 = one SD

set.seed(853)
train <- sample(nrow(X), 479)   # 80% to train; the other 120 lines are for testing
test  <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), train)

rmse <- function(pred, actual) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))

# Least squares on the chosen marker columns; returns one row of the results table
ls_row <- function(columns) {
  fit   <- lm(y[train] ~ X[train, columns])
  coefs <- coef(fit)
  used  <- sum(!is.na(coefs)) - 1   # markers lm could estimate (not counting the intercept)
  coefs[is.na(coefs)] <- 0          # lm returns NA for markers it can't estimate
  data.frame(method         = "Least squares",
             markers_chosen = length(columns),
             markers_used   = used,
             train_rmse     = sqrt(mean(resid(fit)^2)),
             test_rmse      = rmse(cbind(1, X[test, columns]) %*% coefs, y[test]))
}

# Ridge or the lasso; returns one row of the results table
shrink_row <- function(fit, name) {
  data.frame(method         = name,
             markers_chosen = ncol(X),
             markers_used   = sum(coef(fit)[-1] != 0),
             train_rmse     = rmse(predict(fit, X[train, ]), y[train]),
             test_rmse      = rmse(predict(fit, X[test, ]), y[test]))
}

# Print ordinary numbers rounded, and huge ones in scientific notation
show_table <- function(results) {
  show_rmse <- function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, format(x, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2), round(x, 2))
  results$train_rmse <- show_rmse(results$train_rmse)
  results$test_rmse  <- show_rmse(results$test_rmse)
  results
}

# Ridge and the lasso use all 1,279 markers, each with its own fixed lambda
# (the lambda values were chosen by cross-validation; Section 3 shows why the choice matters)
ridge <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = 34)
lasso <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 1, lambda = 0.48)
shrink_rows <- rbind(shrink_row(ridge, "Ridge"), shrink_row(lasso, "Lasso"))

# Least squares gets all the markers, sorted by their individual R-squared with yield
r2     <- cor(X[train, ], y[train])^2
ranked <- order(r2, decreasing = TRUE)

show_table(rbind(ls_row(ranked), shrink_rows))
```

> **YOUR TURN:** Try different numbers of features for least squares,
> ranked by each marker's individual R-squared with yield on the
> training lines. Edit `n_markers` and run the chunk to print the
> results. Ridge and the lasso stay the same, for comparison.

```{r}
n_markers <- c(1, 1279)   # <- change me (add to the list)

library(glmnet)
data(wheat, package = "BGLR")   # loads wheat.X (markers) and wheat.Y (yield)
X <- wheat.X
y <- 100 + 10 * wheat.Y[, 1]    # yield index: 100 = average line, 10 = one SD

set.seed(853)
train <- sample(nrow(X), 479)   # 80% to train; the other 120 lines are for testing
test  <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), train)

rmse <- function(pred, actual) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))

# Rank markers by their individual R-squared with yield on the training lines
r2     <- cor(X[train, ], y[train])^2
ranked <- order(r2, decreasing = TRUE)

# Least squares on the top k markers
ls_row <- function(k) {
  columns <- ranked[1:k]
  fit     <- lm(y[train] ~ X[train, columns])
  coefs   <- coef(fit)
  used    <- sum(!is.na(coefs)) - 1   # markers lm could estimate (not counting the intercept)
  coefs[is.na(coefs)] <- 0            # lm returns NA for markers it can't estimate
  data.frame(method         = "Least squares",
             markers_chosen = k,
             markers_used   = used,
             train_rmse     = sqrt(mean(resid(fit)^2)),
             test_rmse      = rmse(cbind(1, X[test, columns]) %*% coefs, y[test]))
}

# Ridge or the lasso on all 1,279 markers
shrink_row <- function(alpha, lambda, name) {
  fit <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = alpha, lambda = lambda)
  data.frame(method         = name,
             markers_chosen = ncol(X),
             markers_used   = sum(coef(fit)[-1] != 0),
             train_rmse     = rmse(predict(fit, X[train, ]), y[train]),
             test_rmse      = rmse(predict(fit, X[test, ]), y[test]))
}

# The lambda values were chosen by cross-validation; Section 3 shows why the choice matters
results <- rbind(do.call(rbind, lapply(n_markers, ls_row)),
                 shrink_row(alpha = 0, lambda = 34, "Ridge"),
                 shrink_row(alpha = 1, lambda = 0.48, "Lasso"))
results$train_rmse <- round(results$train_rmse, 2)
results$test_rmse  <- round(results$test_rmse, 2)
results
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The point"}
When many features each have a small effect, ridge predicts best: it
keeps every marker and shrinks them all. Least squares on all the
markers fits the training lines perfectly and predicts new lines badly.
Using only the top-ranked markers stops the blow-up, but it doesn't
catch ridge.
:::

## 2. Yield of a Chemical Manufacturing Process

These data come from a 27-step process that makes a pharmaceutical
product.

- **Rows:** 176 samples of the process.
- **Features:** 57 measurements: 12 of the biological starting material,
  and 45 of the manufacturing process, such as temperature, drying time,
  and washing time.
- **Response:** percent yield of the final product.

We train on 80% of the samples (141) and test on the other 20% (35).

> **PREDICT:** Suppose only a few of these 57 measurements really drive
> yield. Which method will predict yield best on the test samples: least
> squares, ridge, or the lasso? Why?

```{r}
#| results: hold
library(glmnet)
data(ChemicalManufacturingProcess, package = "AppliedPredictiveModeling")
X <- as.matrix(ChemicalManufacturingProcess[, -1])   # the 57 measurements
y <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess$Yield              # percent yield

set.seed(8)
train <- sample(nrow(X), 141)   # 80% to train; the other 35 samples are for testing
test  <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), train)

# Some measurements are missing: fill each with its median on the training samples
for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) {
  X[is.na(X[, j]), j] <- median(X[train, j], na.rm = TRUE)
}

rmse <- function(pred, actual) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))

# Least squares on all the features
ls_fit  <- lm(y[train] ~ X[train, ])
coefs   <- coef(ls_fit)
ls_used <- sum(!is.na(coefs)) - 1   # features lm could estimate (not counting the intercept)
coefs[is.na(coefs)] <- 0            # lm returns NA for features it can't estimate

# Ridge or the lasso on all the features; returns one row of the results table
shrink_row <- function(alpha, lambda, name) {
  fit <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = alpha, lambda = lambda)
  data.frame(method        = name,
             features_used = sum(coef(fit)[-1] != 0),
             train_rmse    = rmse(predict(fit, X[train, ]), y[train]),
             test_rmse     = rmse(predict(fit, X[test, ]), y[test]))
}

# The lambda values were chosen by cross-validation; Section 3 shows why the choice matters
results <- rbind(
  data.frame(method        = "Least squares",
             features_used = ls_used,
             train_rmse    = sqrt(mean(resid(ls_fit)^2)),
             test_rmse     = rmse(cbind(1, X[test, ]) %*% coefs, y[test])),
  shrink_row(alpha = 0, lambda = 3.1, "Ridge"),
  shrink_row(alpha = 1, lambda = 0.071, "Lasso")
)
results$train_rmse <- round(results$train_rmse, 2)
results$test_rmse  <- round(results$test_rmse, 2)
base::print.data.frame(results)   # plain text, so the table and the summary show together
cat("\n")

# How many features did the lasso zero out, and what kind did it keep?
lasso       <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 1, lambda = 0.071)
lasso_coefs <- as.matrix(coef(lasso))[-1, ]   # leave out the intercept
is_bio      <- grepl("Biological", names(lasso_coefs))

cat("The lasso zeroed out ", sum(lasso_coefs == 0), " of ", length(lasso_coefs), " features.\n",
    "It kept ", sum(lasso_coefs[is_bio] != 0), " of ", sum(is_bio),
    " biological measurements (quality and characteristics of the starting material)\n",
    "and ", sum(lasso_coefs[!is_bio] != 0), " of ", sum(!is_bio),
    " process measurements (such as temperature, drying time, and washing time).\n", sep = "")
```

> **YOUR TURN:** Try different numbers of features for least squares,
> ranked by each feature's individual R-squared with yield on the
> training samples. Edit `n_features` and run the chunk to print the
> results. Ridge and the lasso stay the same, for comparison.

```{r}
n_features <- c(1, 57)   # <- change me (add to the list)

library(glmnet)
data(ChemicalManufacturingProcess, package = "AppliedPredictiveModeling")
X <- as.matrix(ChemicalManufacturingProcess[, -1])   # the 57 measurements
y <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess$Yield              # percent yield

set.seed(8)
train <- sample(nrow(X), 141)   # 80% to train; the other 35 samples are for testing
test  <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), train)

# Some measurements are missing: fill each with its median on the training samples
for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) {
  X[is.na(X[, j]), j] <- median(X[train, j], na.rm = TRUE)
}

rmse <- function(pred, actual) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))

# Rank features by their individual R-squared with yield on the training samples
r2     <- cor(X[train, ], y[train])^2
ranked <- order(r2, decreasing = TRUE)

# Least squares on the top k features
ls_row <- function(k) {
  columns <- ranked[1:k]
  fit     <- lm(y[train] ~ X[train, columns])
  coefs   <- coef(fit)
  used    <- sum(!is.na(coefs)) - 1   # features lm could estimate (not counting the intercept)
  coefs[is.na(coefs)] <- 0            # lm returns NA for features it can't estimate
  data.frame(method          = "Least squares",
             features_chosen = k,
             features_used   = used,
             train_rmse      = sqrt(mean(resid(fit)^2)),
             test_rmse       = rmse(cbind(1, X[test, columns]) %*% coefs, y[test]))
}

# Ridge or the lasso on all 57 features
shrink_row <- function(alpha, lambda, name) {
  fit <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = alpha, lambda = lambda)
  data.frame(method          = name,
             features_chosen = ncol(X),
             features_used   = sum(coef(fit)[-1] != 0),
             train_rmse      = rmse(predict(fit, X[train, ]), y[train]),
             test_rmse       = rmse(predict(fit, X[test, ]), y[test]))
}

# The lambda values were chosen by cross-validation; Section 3 shows why the choice matters
results <- rbind(do.call(rbind, lapply(n_features, ls_row)),
                 shrink_row(alpha = 0, lambda = 3.1, "Ridge"),
                 shrink_row(alpha = 1, lambda = 0.071, "Lasso"))
results$train_rmse <- round(results$train_rmse, 2)
results$test_rmse  <- round(results$test_rmse, 2)
results
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The point"}
When a few features carry most of the signal, the lasso predicts best
and drops many features along the way. Here, least squares on a short
list of top-ranked features nearly matches the lasso, which it couldn't
do with ridge on the wheat data.
:::

## 3. Finding the Best λ

Back to the wheat data from Section 1: the same 599 lines, 1,279 genetic
markers, and yield index. This time we fit ridge at 200 values of
$\lambda$ and average the test error at each one over 10 random 80/20
splits.

> **PREDICT:** As $\lambda$ grows from almost zero to very large, what
> shape will the test error follow?

```{r}
library(glmnet)
library(ggplot2)
data(wheat, package = "BGLR")   # loads wheat.X (markers) and wheat.Y (yield)
X <- wheat.X
y <- 100 + 10 * wheat.Y[, 1]    # yield index: 100 = average line, 10 = one SD

# Plot average test RMSE across lambda for one method: alpha = 0 is ridge, alpha = 1 is the lasso
plot_lambda_curve <- function(alpha) {
  lambdas <- 10^seq(5, -3, length.out = 200)   # 200 values, from very large to very small

  # Test RMSE at each lambda, for one random 80/20 split
  split_rmse <- function(seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    train <- sample(nrow(X), 479)   # 80% to train; the other 120 lines are for testing
    test  <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), train)
    fit   <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = alpha, lambda = lambdas)
    preds <- predict(fit, X[test, ], s = lambdas)
    sqrt(colMeans((preds - y[test])^2))
  }

  # Average over 10 random splits, and find the lambda where the average is lowest
  errors <- data.frame(lambda = lambdas, test_rmse = rowMeans(sapply(1:10, split_rmse)))
  best   <- errors[which.min(errors$test_rmse), ]

  ggplot(errors, aes(lambda, test_rmse)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
    geom_point(data = best, size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(data = best, vjust = 2,
              aes(label = sprintf("Minimum: lambda = %.3g, test RMSE = %.2f", lambda, test_rmse))) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^(-3:5),
                  labels = format(10^(-3:5), scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE,
                                  trim = TRUE, big.mark = ",")) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = pretty(c(best$test_rmse - 0.6, errors$test_rmse), n = 12)) +
    expand_limits(y = best$test_rmse - 0.6) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = if (alpha == 0) "Ridge" else if (alpha == 1) "Lasso" else paste0("Elastic-Net (alpha = ", alpha, ")"),
         x = "lambda (log scale)", y = "Average test RMSE (yield points)")
}

plot_lambda_curve(alpha = 0)   # ridge is alpha = 0, lasso is alpha = 1
```

> **YOUR TURN:** Change `alpha` to the value for the lasso and run this
> chunk. How does the best $\lambda$ compare with ridge's?

```{r}
# ridge is alpha = 0, lasso is alpha = 1
plot_lambda_curve(alpha = 0)   # <- change me to lasso regularization
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The point"}
Test error falls and then rises as $\lambda$ grows. Too little shrinkage
leaves high variance, too much adds bias, and the best $\lambda$ is in
between. The best value is very different for ridge and the lasso, so it
has to be chosen separately for each method, which is what
cross-validation does.
:::
